Occupational injuries pose a substantial big health and economic challenge worldwide, particularly in the construction industry, which is characterized by inherently hazardous working conditions. Despite rapid growth of the construction sector and the implementation of occupational safety policies in Rwanda, injury rates remain high, especially in urban centers such as Kigali City.
1. Determine the prevalence: Estimate the prevalence of occupational injuries among building construction workers in Kigali city.
2. Identify risk factors: Identify the risk factors associated with occupational injuries among building construction workers in Kigali city, including:
Demographic factors age, sex, education level, etc., Occupational factors (type of work, working hours, experience),
,Environmental factors (working conditions, safety equipment, ), Behavioral factors (safety practices, risk-taking behavior, .)
3. Understand the impact: Examine the impact of occupational injuries on the health, well-being, and economic situation of building construction workers in Kigali city.

4. Inform prevention strategies: Provide evidence-based recommendations for the development of effective prevention strategies and interventions to reduce the risk of occupational injuries among building construction workers in Kigali city.
A descriptive cross-sectional study will be conducted between may

among 427 construction workers selected through convenient study. Data will be collected via structured questionnaire, Descriptive statistics, along with bivariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses, will be performed using Stata version 17 to identify factors associated with occupational injuries.

For the purpose of this study, an occupational injury is referred to any physical harm or damage to the body that occurs as a result of a work-related incident or exposure while working on a building construction site in the City of Kigali.
: For the purpose of this study, construction workers refer to individuals who are engaged in physical labor or technical work on building construction sites in the City of Kigali.

: In the context of this study, Personal Protective Equipment refers to specialized clothing or equipment worn by building construction workers in the City of Kigali to prevent or minimize occupational injuries and illnesses.

: In the context of this study, Occupational Health and Safety refers to the practices, policies, and procedures aimed at preventing occupational injuries and illnesses among building construction workers in the City of Kigali.

: In the context of this study, the work environment refers to the physical, social, and organizational conditions that exist on building construction sites in the City of Kigali, which can affect the health, safety, and well-being of construction workers.

: In the context of this study, risk-taking behavior refers to actions or decisions made by building construction workers in the City of Kigali that increase the likelihood of occupational injuries or illnesses.

Prevalence of Occupational Injuries Among Building Construction Workers in Kigali City

In this descriptive cross-sectional study conducted among 423 building construction workers in Kigali City, nearly half of the respondents reported experiencing an occupational injury within the past six months. The overall prevalence of occupational injuries was 49.2% (208/423), while 50.8% (215/423) reported no history of injury during the same period. This indicates a substantial burden of occupational injuries among construction workers in Kigali City at the time of the survey.
Distribution of Occupational Injuries by Socio-Demographic Characteristics

The occurrence of occupational injuries was described across various socio-demographic characteristics of the respondents. Although variations in injury prevalence were observed among different groups, no statistically significant associations were identified (all p-values > 0.05).

Injury prevalence varied across age groups. Workers aged 38–47 years reported the highest prevalence (55.1%), followed by those aged 18–27 years (49.0%) and 28–37 years (48.3%). Workers aged above 47 years had the lowest reported prevalence (33.3%).

By sex, injury prevalence was similar among males (50.0%) and females (47.3%). Regarding marital status, married workers had a prevalence of 50.6%, singles 49.5%, separated/widowed 47.4%, and cohabiting workers 42.5%.
In terms of educational level, workers with no formal education had the highest prevalence (51.4%), followed by primary education (50.7%), tertiary education (50.0%), and secondary education (46.6%).
Based on employment status, casual workers reported the highest injury prevalence (52.2%), followed by temporary workers (48.5%) and permanent workers (44.4%).
With respect to construction experience, workers with 1–4 years of experience had a prevalence of 51.4%, those with more than four years had 50.0%, and those with less than one year reported 45.9%.
Overall, while differences were observed across socio-demographic categories, the distribution suggests relatively comparable injury occurrence among most groups.
Distribution of Occupational Injuries by Behavioral Characteristics
The prevalence of occupational injuries was also described according to behavioral characteristics.

Workers who reported alcohol consumption had a higher injury prevalence (62.3%) compared to non-drinkers (35.3%). Similarly, those who reported drinking alcohol before work had a notably higher prevalence (73.8%) compared to those who did not (51.5%).

Smoking was associated with higher injury prevalence, with 64.6% of smokers reporting injuries compared to 46.8% of non-smokers. Workers who experienced trouble sleeping reported an injury prevalence of 62.7%, compared to 44.6% among those without sleep problems.

Workers who reported experiencing work-related stress had a prevalence of 56.1%, while those without stress had a prevalence of 40.6%. Additionally, workers who engaged in risk-taking behaviors at work had a higher injury prevalence (62.8%) compared to those who did not (40.6%).
These findings indicate noticeable differences in injury occurrence across behavioral categories in this cross-sectional assessment.
Distribution of Occupational Injuries by Work Environment Characteristics

Work environment-related characteristics were also described in relation to injury occurrence. Variations in injury prevalence were observed across categories; however, no statistically significant associations were identified (all p-values > 0.05).
Workers who never used personal protective equipment (PPE) reported the highest injury prevalence (80.0%), compared to those who sometimes used PPE (47.7%) and those who always used PPE (49.2%).
Workers who had received safety training reported an injury prevalence of 49.7%, while those without training reported 43.2%.
Regarding daily working hours, injury prevalence was 44.4% among those working
8 hours, 51.3% among those working 9–10 hours, and 36.4% among those working more than 10 hours.

Injury prevalence was similar across night shift categories: sometimes (48.6%), often (46.7%), and never (49.6%). Workers who reported the presence of a written safety policy at the site had an injury prevalence of 50.3%, compared to 35.7% among those reporting no policy.

Similarly, injury prevalence was 50.1% where hazard signs were present and 34.8% where they were absent. With regard to supervision quality, injury prevalence was 50.0% among those reporting adequate supervision, 48.4% among those reporting inadequate supervision, and 33.3% among those reporting no supervision.
By job role, carpenters had the highest injury prevalence (57.1%), followed by masons (53.4%), other roles (50.0%), and laborers (44.5%).

In the adjusted binary logistic regression model, drinking alcohol before work remained the only factor independently associated with occupational injury.

Workers who reported drinking alcohol before work had 2.14 times higher odds of sustaining an occupational injury compared to those who did not drink before work (AOR = 2.14, 95% CI: 1.11–4.14, p = 0.024).
Other behavioral variables, including alcohol consumption during work, smoking status, sleep problems, stress, and risk-taking behavior, did not retain statistical significance in the adjusted model.

This study showed a high prevalence of occupational injuries among building construction workers in Kigali City, with nearly half of the respondents reporting injury within the preceding six months. Behavioral factors, particularly alcohol consumption before work, were identified as significant predictors of injury risk. Workers who consumed alcohol prior to starting work had more than twice the odds of sustaining an occupational injury compared to those who did not. While other behavioral factors such as smoking, sleep disturbances, work-related stress, and risk-taking behaviors showed associations in bivariate analyses, they were not independently significant after adjustment.

Reducing occupational injuries among construction workers in Kigali City requires a comprehensive, multi-stakeholder approach focused on behavioral risk factors. Policymakers should prioritize strengthening the enforcement of occupational health and safety regulations, with particular attention to behavioral hazards such as alcohol consumption before and during work hours. The development and implementation of national policies addressing substance use in the construction sector will provide clear standards for both employers and employees. Moreover, integrating behavioral risk assessments and targeted interventions into existing occupational health frameworks is essential to enhance preventive measures and ensure safer workplaces.

Employers and industry stakeholders have a pivotal role in fostering a culture of safety by instituting regular workplace health promotion programs. These programs should emphasize reducing alcohol use, promoting smoking cessation, managing work-related stress, and discouraging risk-taking behaviors. Comprehensive safety training that highlights the dangers of alcohol consumption before work and raises awareness of behavioral risks should be routinely provided.

Finally, engaging workers directly in safety efforts is critical. Increasing awareness about the risks associated with alcohol use before work and other behavioral hazards, along with encouraging active participation in safety and health promotion initiatives, will empower workers to make safer choices and reduce their injury risk.
